catalog_citation: Haldeman, S. S. 1872. Pennsylvania Dutch: A Dialect of South German with an Infusion of English. London: Truebner & Co. (archive.org bub_gb_M2gCAAAAQAAJ, djvu text layer).
catalog_locator: Ch. II (phonology), closing paragraph, p. 16 (djvu text line ~1630); cf. footnote in the reading selections (djvu line ~4301) on ee'mool/emool.
catalog_quote: The length of some vowels is doubtful, as in ' rot' or 'root' (red, like English röte or rode), 'so' or ' soo,' ' nochbar ' or 'noochbar,' ' amol ' or ' emool,' ... Accent in PG. agrees with that of High German. When indicated^ as in danöot or danoot' (for the ' oo ' represent a single [v]owel, as in Eng. f[l]oor), it is to afford aid to the reader not [fa]miliar [with] German accent

audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote confirmed verbatim (scanned-noisy) at lines 1630-1633, p.16 end of Ch. II, exactly as cited. (2) The deciding source is an 1872 69-page sketch whose accent statement defers wholesale to High German; it is not the best available description — Glottolog 5.1 and OpenLibrary list a dedicated phonology monograph (Kelz 1971), Reed 1947/1949 phonologies, the standard grammar Buffington & Barba 1954, Frey 1942, Haag 1982 and Van Ness 1994, none held and none open (Reed 1949/Haag 1982 lending-only on archive.org; search-inside 403). (3) Nothing suggests the classification is wrong: PG is a Palatinate-derived German dialect and every held/downloaded primary text that marks accent (Haldeman's texts, Hoffman 1889 headwords, Lambert 1924 entries) shows German-type stem accent with unstressed be-/ge-/er-/ver- prefixes and idiosyncratic loans — 'lexical', not computable from syllable c
audit.second_reader_evidence: QUOTE: re-confirmed verbatim (scanned noise only) in the copy we hold lines 1630-1633: 'Accent in PG. agrees with that of High German. When indicated^ as in danöot or danoot' (for the ' oo * represent a single Towel, as in Eng.^foor), it is to afford aid to the reader not ^miliar ifiih German accent' — the record's bracketed repairs are right. The preceding vowel-length sentence ('rot'/'root'.. 'amol'/'emool') is at lines 1607-1623. Page: bare '16' at line 1243 and '17' at line 1645 immediately after the passage (followed by 'GHAPTEB III.'), so p.16, closing paragraph of Ch. II, exactly

sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: No placement rule stated; accent is marked on every headword with an acute. Marks show stem-initial accent with unstressed prefixes (ar- = er-, ba- = be-, far- = ver-) and non-initial accent in some loans, i.e. High-German-type lexical/morphological accent.
sources.locator: orthography key, djvu line ~185 ('the acute accent is employed to indicate accented syllables, as riv'er, re-tere''); vocabulary headwords passim (e.g. ar-fa'-rung, ba-ding'-a, a-bart'-ich vs. ar'-mut, e'-lendt)

sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request); access check: open copy online
sources.note: The archive.org item (Leiden University theses collection) is the printed 16-page ABSTRACT of Frey's 1941 Illinois dissertation, not the 478-page dissertation itself. Its Part One (Phonology) lists the phoneme inventory and MHG correspondences and says nothing about accent or stress placement; a full-text search for stress/accent|accent|betont finds only the 'unstressed dR' pronoun note. The full dissertation (UIUC IDEALS) was could not be reached by automated download in the earlier reading. Same variety: Eastern York County (Lower Windsor Township) Pennsylvania German.
